H1.text: A cook in Chennai and a cook in Delhi both weigh one kilogram of rice. Every watch counts the same second.

H2.text: They never met. So how do they agree on exactly how much a kilogram or a second is?

H3.text: Aarav finds out the hard way. His spanner is marked thirteen millimetres.

H4.text: His bicycle bolt is half an inch, twelve point seven millimetres. The spanner slips.

H5.text: A gap of just zero point three millimetres. That is why the world agreed on one set of units.

P1.text: That set is called SI, the International System of Units.

P2.text: It has seven base units, one for each base quantity.

P3.text: Metre for length. Kilogram for mass. Second for time. Ampere for electric current.

P4.text: Kelvin for temperature. Mole for amount of substance. Candela for luminous intensity.

P5.text: Every other unit is built from these seven. Those are derived units.

S1.text: But who decides how long one metre is? Let's watch light do it.

S2.text: Light in vacuum always travels at the same speed: two hundred ninety nine million, seven hundred ninety two thousand, four hundred fifty eight metres per second.

S3.text: So one metre is the distance light travels in that tiny fraction of a second: one part in this exact number.

S4.text: Watch the pulse cross one metre. The clock reads about three point three four nanoseconds.

S5.text: Slow motion. The blue arrow is the speed of light. It never changes, so the graph is a straight line.

S6.text: Its slope is c. Same light, same metre, anywhere.

L1.text: The other base units are tied to fixed numbers of nature too.

L2.text: The second comes from the caesium atom: nine billion, one hundred ninety two million, six hundred thirty one thousand, seven hundred seventy ticks.

L3.text: The kilogram is fixed by the Planck constant. Until twenty nineteen, it was a metal cylinder near Paris.

L4.text: Nature's numbers never change, so the units never drift.

D1.text: Now let's build a derived unit step by step. The joule, the unit of work and energy.

D2.text: Step one. Force equals mass times acceleration. So one newton is one kilogram metre per second squared.

D3.text: Step two. Work equals force times distance. So one joule is one newton times one metre.

D4.text: Step three. Put the newton in. One joule is one kilogram metre squared per second squared.

D5.text: Every named unit hides base units. The pascal is newton per square metre. The watt is joule per second.

T1.text: Remember this. Seven base units. Every other unit is built from them.

K1.text: Side by side. The kilogram is a base unit. Chosen, not built.

K2.text: The newton is derived. It has its own name, but inside it is kilogram, metre and second.

K3.text: Now you try. The watt is named after a scientist, like the newton. Base unit or derived unit? Pause and decide.

K4.text: Derived! A watt is one joule per second. Open it, and you get kilogram metre squared per second cubed.

R1.text: SI also has rules for writing units. Exams love them.

R2.text: Unit names are written in small letters, even when named after a person. The unit newton has a small n.

R3.text: But the symbol of a person's unit is a capital. N for newton, Pa for pascal, K for kelvin.

R4.text: Other symbols stay small: m, s, kg.

R5.text: No plural, and no full stop. Five kilograms is five k g, never five K g s.

R6.text: Your turn. A label says five capital K g. Is that correct? Pause and decide.

R7.text: No! Capital K is the kelvin, a temperature. The kilogram is small k, small g.

W2.text: Aarav pushes his bicycle with twenty newtons for fifteen metres. Find the work done in base units.

W3.text: Work equals force times distance: twenty newtons times fifteen metres.

W4.text: That is three hundred newton metres, or three hundred joules.

W5.text: Now open the joule: kilogram metre squared per second squared.

W6.text: So the work is three hundred kilogram metre squared per second squared.

X2.text: Many students say the gram is the SI base unit of mass, because kilo is just a prefix.

X3.text: But the SI base unit of mass is the kilogram. It is the only base unit with a prefix in its name.

E1.text: Where is this asked? As one mark questions: a unit in base units, the base unit, or the wrong symbol.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Sunlight intensity is measured in joule per second per square metre. What is this in SI base units? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is A. Kilogram per second cubed.

A2.text: Joule per second is the watt: kilogram metre squared per second cubed. That is B, but we are not done.

A3.text: Divide by square metre. The metre squared cancels: kilogram per second cubed. C is the pascal, and D keeps a stray metre.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. How is the metre defined today?

Y3.text: Two. Write the joule using only base units.

Y4.text: Three. Why is five K g wrong?

N1.text: Next time: the tyre says psi, the pump says bar. Why do other unit systems still exist? We find out in systems of units.
